top_evidence.document_title: A patient-centered approach to inclusive AI in healthcare: potential benefits, challenges, and recommendations
top_evidence.section: Data Items And Data Extraction > Methods
top_evidence.text: All selected articles were included in qualitative synthesis and were divided between two authors (EG and KD), with each author extracting data from half of the articles. After which further discussion was carried out among the three authors during data extraction. The following information was extracted from each study: Healthcare context (e.g., condition, medical specialty); Type of AI solution (e.g., AI-based prediction algorithm, natural language processing, chatbot); Use of frameworks and/or guidelines to ensure inclusivity in AI; Specific methods for implementing inclusivity within the AI solution; and the discussed SWOT data addressing the strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats of inclusive AI solutions. The classification of discussed topics into SWOT categories was based on the characteristics highlighted in each article. When the categorization was explicitly stated by the authors, it was directly adopted. When not clearly reported, positive characteristics already in place and described positively were classified as Strengths, while positive characteristics expected to occur were classified as Opportunities. Negative characteristics that have already occurred were classified as Weaknesses, and negative characteristics anticipated to occur were classified as Threats. These classifications were performed by the author responsible for extracting the data. In this study, a literature review was adopted as the chosen research approach by carrying out a systematic review with conceptual synthesis, following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines [21], as seen in Appendix 3. We searched six databases (PubMed, PsycINFO, CINAHL, Academic Search Premier, IEEE Xplore, and Scopus) for publications that included the keyword 'Inclusive AI' in their abstract. In this study we prioritize the literature to explicitly addressing 'inclusive AI' in healthcare as this area has not been well addressed in prior studies. Accordingly, we used only the keyword 'Inclusive AI' 'strategies', 'solutions', 'regulatory frameworks', 'applications', 'benefits', 'challenges', AND 'bias', 'fair - ness', 'equity', OR 'diversity' AND 'healthcare' to ensure the search captured publications where inclusivity was an explicit and central focus. The search was conducted on the 26th of September 2024. The search was carried out again on the 16th of April 2026 after extending the search keyword based on the research questions being examined in this study to improve the literature. The full search strategy can be found in Appendix 1. We uploaded all identified refer - ences to EndNote, removed duplicates, and then uploaded the remaining references to Rayyan.

top_evidence.section: Frameworks To Ensure Inclusivity, Methods And Definitions Of Inclusive Ai
top_evidence.text: Several frameworks and guidelines supporting inclusive AI were reported in the included articles. One article referred to the ACCEPT-AI, SPIRIT-AI, and CONSORT-AI frameworks [33]. Another article discussed a Bias Mitigation Framework and ethical AI design principles [8], while one highlighted the FAIR, FACT, and RE-AIM frameworks [31]. Maheshwari et al. referred to a framework of institutional epistemic trust [32], and Israni et al. mentioned a human rights values framework [25]. Tielman et al. outlined the IEEE 7000 standard for ethical system design, W3C Accessibility Guidelines, and a socio-cognitive engineering method [34]. Doo and McGinty referred to the 'digital determinants of health' sociotechnical framework [27], while Dekker et al., mentioned the Braun and Matthes framework for chatbot classification and several technol - ogy acceptance theories [24]. Ekellem and Köhler referred to GUI (Graphical User Interface) principles [28], and Denecke et al. discussed Just-in-Time Adaptive Intervention design [9]. One article highlighted the principles of distributive justice [5], and another one referred to Sustainable Development Goal 17 of the United Nations ('Partnership for the Goals') [22]. Rubeis et al. mentioned the Social Justice Framework for Bridging the Digital Divide and Health Equity Impact Assessment [26], while one article discussed the Ubuntu philosophy [6]. Four articles [1, 23, 29, 30] did not mention any specific framework or guideline for ensur - ing inclusive AI. We extracted several threats from the papers. Bias in AI algorithms, underrepresentation of marginalized groups, and exclusion of low-income regions contribute to unequal healthcare access and outcomes. These disparities can reinforce existing inequities, leading to poorer health results for disadvantaged populations. AI-driven healthcare faces challenges related to data privacy, commercial exploitation, and the absence of clear consent mechanisms. Misuse of patient data to train AI models raises ethical and legal concerns, potentially eroding trust in AI applications. Overreliance on AI technologies may lead to diminished clinical skills among healthcare professionals and oversimplifica - tion of complex medical decision-making. Inadequate infrastructure, governance gaps, and global disparities hinder the seamless adoption of AI in healthcare. Resource-poor regions may struggle to implement AI solutions effectively, exacerbating existing inequalities. Resistance to AI adoption stems from fears of AI replacing human judgement, ethical dilemmas, and a lack of public trust. Concerns about accountability, transparency and fairness further slow the adoption of AI in medical decision making. From these threats, the most commonly discussed threat identified from the selected and reviewed sources was the exacerbation of inequities, noted in 14 articles, warning that biases in algorithms and exclusion of low-income regions could further widen health disparities [5, 6, 8, 9, 22, 23, 26-31, 33, 34]. top_evidence.text: The search resulted in 1,377 results. After removing duplicates in EndNote and Rayyan, we kept 1,163 results for further screening. In the title and abstract screening, both reviewers agreed to exclude 1,124 references; 39 articles were considered appropriate to be screened in depth during full-text review. Twenty-one were excluded at this stage; the list of excluded articles during the full-text screening and the reason for their exclusion is presented in Appendix 2. A total of 18 articles were included in this review [1, 5, 6, 8, 9, 22-34] (see Fig. 1, and Table 1). All included articles were published between 2020 and 2024. top_evidence.document_title: A patient-centered approach to inclusive AI in healthcare: potential benefits, challenges, and recommendations
top_evidence.text: From the results, we derived facets of inclusive AI solutions in healthcare, formulated recommendations addressing these facets to achieve inclusive AI in healthcare and formulated a research agenda. In order to assess eligibility, two authors (EG and KD) independently screened the titles and abstracts of all identified articles. In the second step, two authors (EG and AJB) independently assessed the eligibility of the selected articles from the first step by reviewing their full text. Any disagree - ments were discussed with a third author (KD) until consensus was reached.
